title: Evan Mobley for Giannis? Trade sounds unlikely as Cavs seem poised to bring back stars
content:
INDEPENDENCE, Ohio — Calling Evan Mobley “part of our future” and a “franchise-caliber player,” Cleveland Cavaliers president of basketball operations Koby Altman’s words should cast serious doubt on one of the hottest rumored moves coming in the NBA’s offseason.

Mobley for Giannis Antetokounmpo? Seems unlikely after Altman’s season-ending review on Friday.

“I’m not going to speculate on any players outside these walls,” Altman said in his first public comments after the Cavs were swept out of the Eastern Conference finals by the New York Knicks. “All I can tell you is, since Evan’s been here, we’ve had the third-best record in the league for five years. Now, we don’t have a championship to show for that yet, right? Boston and Denver, the other two ahead of us, they have a championship to show for that, but all Evan has done is impact winning. He’s been remarkable for us in terms of our ascent the last five years. He’s a huge part of what we do.”

The Cavs reached the conference finals for the first time since 2018 and the first time without LeBron James on the roster since 1992. They also had the NBA’s most expensive roster, ever, at $229 million before taxes, and are on pace to pay 12 players $224.5 million next season — notable in part because there could be up to 17 players on the roster.

Altman said the Cavs would consider a move to cut salary and get under the salary aprons — which are projected to be $209 million (first apron) and $222 million (second apron) — if “it makes sense to do it.” Teams over those apron lines are greatly restricted in how they can make roster changes.

“There’s no urgency to get out of (the aprons) just to get out of (them),” Altman added, “because then you’d be shedding contracts and good players to do it.”

Altman said the only directive from team owner Dan Gilbert is to improve, which could happen internally, or through moves made “around the edges” or a “big ticket move. We’re going to look at all of it.”

So there it is, the window left slightly ajar for the Cavs to make easily the splashiest trade of the summer. But otherwise, everything Altman said about Mobley made it sound certain they will keep him.

Mobley is 24 and will make $50.1 million next season. He is most commonly linked to a Giannis trade because:

But Altman said Mobley “was consistently our best player throughout the playoffs,” and said the next step for Mobley is to add muscle and girth to his lanky frame. Altman said the Cavs are “very fortunate to have drafted Evan” out of a deep 2021 draft class that also includes Toronto’s Scottie Barnes, Detroit’s Cade Cunningham and Orlando’s Franz Wagner.

“Out of those guys, who’s the first to the conference finals? Evan Mobley,” Altman said; the Cavs beat Barnes’ Raptors in Round 1 and Cunningham’s Pistons in Round 2. “We have to be proud of that. We have to take pride in that. It’s easy to knock someone down. … He’s a franchise-caliber player and we’re very fortunate to have him.”

Altman also said of Mobley and his Cleveland frontcourt mate, Jarrett Allen: “Those two fit really well together, and, and we’re excited about their future together.”

So if those comments are meant to be taken at face value, then the Cavs should be expected to hold onto not only Mobley, but Allen also.

As for the team’s resident current superstar, Donovan Mitchell, Altman called him “uniquely our own” and “our guy.” Mitchell, 29, can be offered a four-year, $277 million extension on July 7. If Mitchell waits until after next season for a new contract, the Cavs could bump him up to the 35-percent max as a 10-year vet, something in the five-year, $352 million range, but it would require the Cavs to allow him to become a free agent first.

Asked about the mechanics of their dealings with Mitchell — extend him now, but if he wants to wait, would the Cavs be comfortable with that? — Altman said, “All I could tell you is Donovan has been steadfast in how much he loves it here. And so there hasn’t been any question of will he be here and does he want to be here?”

Translation: Mitchell isn’t going anywhere.

Which leaves James Harden, acquired at the February trade deadline, as the last “big ticket” caliber player who the Cavs could use as a piece to change the roster. But that one also sounds highly unlikely. Harden said after the Game 4 loss to New York that “100 percent” he hoped, and planned, to be in Cleveland next season, and Altman echoed those sentiments on Friday.

Harden, who turns 37 in August, has a $42.3 million player option on his current contract for next season, which is partially guaranteed for $13.3 million until July 11. It means that if Harden were to pick up his option by June 29 (the deadline to do so), and the Cavs waived him before July 11, they would only be on the hook for $13.3 million. He is widely expected to decline the option and sign a new deal with the Cavs — when that happens, he can’t be traded over the summer.

As previously reported by The Athletic, coach Kenny Atkinson is returning for a third season, also.

To review: Atkinson. Mobley. Mitchell. Harden. Allen. All of them, it sounded Friday, should be expected to return to the Cavs for the 2026-27 season.

Would the Bucks accept, say, a Jimi Hendrix guitar pic from the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame? Several pounds of Lake Erie walleye? How about Myles Garrett from the Cleveland Browns (hey, the Browns’ owner, Jimmy Haslam, also owns the Bucks now)?

Otherwise, it sounds like the Cavs are largely running it back, which would certainly prevent them from trading for Giannis.

“I always say two things can be true — we hated the way it ended, we were disappointed with the way it ended. I think the reason for that is we have higher expectations,” Altman said. “We’ve built this thing to a level of standards of excellence, and we know we could be better.

“But the other thing that could be true is we could be proud of what we’ve accomplished here and be proud of what we’ve built — a very, very strong foundation. We believe in the culture that we built. We believe in the players that we have in house. We have incredible ownership with great resources that helps us achieve in every aspect of this really difficult game that we’re in.”

No one said anything about free agents who used to play in Los Angeles, though.
